title: How GPS depends on Einstein
summary: Position from time signals, why the receiver solves for its own clock bias, the special and general relativistic clock shifts (-7 and +45 microseconds per day), the factory frequency offset, the eccentricity and Sagnac corrections, and ionospheric delay.
questions: Why does a receiver need four satellites rather than three, and what extra thing does it get?
Which relativistic effect is larger for GPS satellites, and which direction does the net effect push their clocks?
If every satellite clock ran fast by the same amount, why would position not drift 10 km a day, and why is relativity still essential?
Why can't the factory frequency offset handle the eccentricity correction, and where is it applied instead?
How does a dual-frequency receiver remove most of the ionospheric delay?

title: Kahneman and Tversky: what they found, and what survived
summary: The partnership, heuristics and biases (representativeness, availability, anchoring, regression to the mean), prospect theory and framing, and which findings survived the replication crisis.
questions: In the Linda problem, why is 'bank teller and feminist' a logical error, and which heuristic explains it?
The flight instructor concluded punishment beats praise. What was actually going on, and why does the mistake reinforce itself?
In the Asian disease problem the options are identical but preferences flip. Explain why using prospect theory.
Why did anchoring and framing survive the replication crisis while social priming mostly didn't? What statistical features separate them?
According to Kahneman and Klein, when can expert intuition be trusted, and does a stock picker's environment qualify?

title: Gödel's incompleteness theorems: what they actually say
summary: Opens with a callback on GPS clock bias. Hilbert's program, Gödel numbering and the diagonal lemma, both incompleteness theorems, the halting-problem route via Turing, and what the theorems don't say (nonstandard models, Presburger arithmetic, Gentzen, Lucas-Penrose).
questions: If the system is consistent, why must the Gödel sentence be true in the ordinary natural numbers, and why isn't it a contradiction that we can see it is true while the system can't prove it?
Gödel also proved first-order logic is complete. How can logic be complete while arithmetic is incomplete? What role do nonstandard models play?
If you add the Gödel sentence or the consistency sentence as a new axiom, why doesn't that rescue completeness?
How does the unsolvability of the halting problem imply incompleteness, and where does the argument use the fact that the axioms are mechanically checkable?
Gentzen proved Peano arithmetic consistent. Why doesn't that contradict the second incompleteness theorem, and why doesn't it fully deliver what Hilbert wanted?

title: Why Bretton Woods collapsed
summary: The 1944 design and the Keynes versus White fight over symmetric adjustment, the short convertible era, Triffin's dilemma as a bank run, the 1960s patches (gold pool, capital controls, two-tier market, SDRs), the Nixon shock and Smithsonian, and the competing explanations for the collapse.
questions: Explain Triffin's dilemma as a bank run. What plays the role of deposits, what plays the role of the vault, and why does the system becoming more successful make it more fragile?
Keynes's plan put pressure on surplus countries as well as deficit countries. Why did the Americans reject that in 1944, and how did the lack of it come back to hurt the system in the late sixties?
Using the trilemma, explain why the growth of the eurodollar market made the fixed pegs harder to hold, and why a doubted peg becomes a one-way bet for speculators.
Why did the collapse of the London Gold Pool in 1968, and the two-tier market that replaced it, amount to a major retreat even though the official price stayed at $35?

Under a fixed exchange rate system anchored on the dollar, how did rising American inflation in the late sixties get transmitted to countries like Germany, and why did that give them a reason to stop holding dollars?

title: How the grid holds 60 hertz, and how Texas nearly lost it
summary: Frequency as the grid's real-time supply-demand ledger, inertia and the swing equation, governor droop and automatic generation control, under-frequency load shedding, what actually failed in Texas in February 2021, and how inverter-based grids replace inertia on purpose.
questions: Why does grid frequency drop when load exceeds generation? Where does the missing energy come from in the first few seconds, and why does that make frequency a system-wide signal of the supply and demand balance?

Using the swing equation, why does replacing half of a grid's synchronous generation with solar and batteries make the same plant trip more dangerous, even with unchanged total capacity? Which part of the frequency response does it affect, and why?
Why do governors use droop rather than every generator trying to hold exactly 60 hertz? What problem does droop solve, and what does it leave unsolved that automatic generation control fixes?

Why is deliberately cutting power to customers the protective response when frequency falls too far? Describe the feedback loop load shedding interrupts, including how low frequency attacks a thermal plant's ability to keep running.

In Texas in 2021, how did the natural gas system and the electric system make each other's failures worse, and why does that interdependence make a cold snap more dangerous than a count of frozen equipment suggests?

title: Why chord progressions work: the guitar as a system
summary: Harmonics and roughness (and the Tsimane study on how much consonance preference is learned), the Pythagorean comma and equal temperament, the fretboard as a lattice, Roman-numeral chords, the tritone engine of the five-seven resolution, and why rock's grammar breaks the classical rules.
questions: Why do intervals with simple frequency ratios, like the octave and the fifth, tend to sound smoother than intervals with complicated ratios? Explain the mechanism in terms of harmonics, then explain why the Tsimane study means this mechanism alone doesn't explain why people enjoy resolution.

Why can't any tuning system make every fifth and every octave perfectly pure at the same time? What does equal temperament give up, and what does it gain, by dividing the octave into twelve identical ratios?
On a guitar, why can you slide a chord shape up the neck and get the same type of chord in a new key? And why does a shape need adjusting when it crosses from the G string to the B string?
Why does the five seven chord pull so strongly to the one chord? Which two notes do the work, what interval do they form, and where does each one move?

Rock progressions often use the flat seven chord in a major key. What does lowering that seventh scale degree remove from the harmony, and why might that make a resolution sound blunter or more settled rather than urgent?

title: How CRISPR finds one sequence among three billion
summary: CRISPR as a bacterial immune system, and the search problem at its core: how Cas9 finds one twenty-letter address in a three-billion-letter genome. The PAM handshake as a cheap reject, the directional R-loop zipper and why seed mismatches matter more, kinetic proofreading via the conformational gate, and why repair pathways (not the cut) decide what you can actually edit. Opens with a callback on GPS clock bias and the dual-frequency ionosphere trick.
questions: Checking for the three-letter handshake only narrows the candidate sites by a factor of about eight, leaving hundreds of millions of positions in the human genome. Explain why this still makes the search tractable. What is the expensive operation that the handshake check protects, and why can the handshake be read without performing it?

Cas9 is much less tolerant of mismatches near the handshake than of mismatches at the far end of the twenty-letter target, even though all twenty positions are logically equivalent as information. Explain the mechanism that creates this asymmetry.

Why is it important that the conformational change licensing the cut happens only after the full-length match forms, rather than the protein cutting as soon as it is stably bound? Frame your answer in terms of what would go wrong with near-matches under the second design.

High-fidelity Cas9 variants are made by weakening the protein's non-specific contacts with the DNA backbone, not by changing the guide RNA. Explain why weakening a non-specific grip improves sequence specificity, and what you give up in exchange.

The sickle cell therapy does not correct the sickle cell mutation. It breaks a regulatory element so that fetal hemoglobin is produced instead. Explain why that indirect approach was easier, in terms of the two DNA repair pathways and which cells they work in.

title: Milgram and the Stanford Prison Experiment: what they showed, and what they didn't
summary: Milgram's obedience studies and their two dozen variations, what the Yale archives revealed (improvised prods, partial disbelief, a direct order that failed), why the Stanford Prison Experiment's famous conclusion collapsed, the BBC Prison Study and truncated replications, and engaged followership as the rival theory.
questions: Across Milgram's variations, obedience ranged from nearly everyone to nearly no one. Pick three of the variations and explain what each one changed, and what that pattern tells you that a single headline number cannot.

Perry and colleagues found that participants who believed the learner was really in pain were more likely to defy the experimenter. Explain why that finding pushes the headline obedience rate in a particular direction, and why a post-experiment questionnaire is still weak evidence on its own.

The fourth prod, 'you have no other choice, you must go on', was the only direct order in Milgram's script, and it was the least effective. Why is that a problem for the agentic state theory, and how does engaged followership explain it?

Explain why the Stanford Prison Experiment, as run, could not support its famous conclusion that roles spontaneously turn ordinary people cruel. Name both a design flaw and something specific the archives revealed.

In the BBC Prison Study, tyranny eventually became a live possibility, but not the way Stanford suggested. What was the mechanism there, and how does it differ from the claim that a role by itself corrupts the person who plays it?

title: The end of Dennard scaling: why clock speeds stopped rising
summary: Why Moore's law (transistor counts) outlived Dennard scaling (constant power density): the constant-field arithmetic, the sixty-millivolt-per-decade Boltzmann limit and gate tunneling that froze voltage, the fixes from high-k metal gates to FinFETs and gate-all-around, and how multicore, dark silicon and specialized accelerators followed.
questions: Under Dennard's constant-field scaling, walk through why power density stays constant. Which term in the dynamic power equation does the heavy lifting, and what happens to power density if voltage is held fixed while everything else scales?
Why does the sixty millivolts per factor of ten limit not improve as transistors get smaller, and why does that limit put a floor under the supply voltage?
High-k dielectrics let the gate insulator get physically thicker. Explain why a thicker layer helps with one problem while preserving performance, and name the leakage problem it does not solve.
What problem does wrapping the gate around more of the channel solve, first with fins and then with nanosheets? Explain the mechanism in terms of who controls the barrier in the channel.

Why can two cores at lower voltage and frequency deliver more throughput than one fast core for the same power, and why did dark silicon push design toward specialized accelerators rather than simply more general-purpose cores?

title: The shipping container: how a steel box rewired the world economy
summary: Why the container only paid off once institutions changed around it: ICC regulation that kept transport modes apart, the committee fight over box sizes and corner fittings, the longshore deals that traded work rules for a share of the gains, port authorities and the Vietnam War, and what the evidence says about its effect on trade and supply-chain fragility.
questions: In the break bulk era, why was the cost of trade concentrated in port rather than at sea, and what exactly did the container eliminate?
Why did the Interstate Commerce Commission's way of regulating transport make the container hard to exploit, and why did McLean have to give up control of his trucking company?
Why did the pioneers, Sea-Land with 35-foot boxes and Matson with 24-foot boxes, end up outside the standard sizes, and why would McLean's company release its corner-fitting patents for free?
What did West Coast longshoremen give up and get in the 1960 Mechanization and Modernization Agreement, and what is the main criticism of that kind of deal?
Why did containerization concentrate shipping in a few giant hub ports rather than spreading it out, and how does that connect to the supply-chain fragility seen during the pandemic?

title: Error-correcting codes: from Shannon's limit to your phone
summary: Shannon's noisy channel theorem and why capacity is a cliff, Hamming's self-locating parity checks, Reed-Solomon polynomials and why erasures cost half what errors do, then turbo codes, Gallager's rediscovered LDPC codes and polar codes in 5G, ending with quantum error correction. Opens with a callback on GPS's eccentricity correction.
questions: Repetition codes can drive the error rate down, so what exactly did Shannon's theorem claim that repetition cannot do, and why does his random coding argument not hand engineers a usable code?

In the seven-four Hamming code, why do three parity checks suffice to locate a single error among seven bits, and what property of the way the checks are assigned makes the syndrome equal to the error's position?

A Reed-Solomon code with a given number of redundant symbols can fix twice as many erasures as errors. Explain why, in terms of unknowns and equations, and explain how interleaving plus erasure flagging lets a CD survive a long scratch.
Why does soft decision decoding beat hard decision decoding, and in an LDPC decoder, why does the parity-check graph need to be sparse for belief propagation to work well?

Quantum mechanics forbids copying an unknown state and disturbs a qubit when you measure it. How does quantum error correction get around both problems, and what is the significance of operating below the error threshold?

title: The science of cooking: why recipes say what they say
summary: Heat as diffusion (time scales with thickness squared), the Maillard reaction and the searing myth, protein denaturation in eggs and meat, how salt and brining really work, emulsions and why mayonnaise is stiff, gluten, leavening and why bread stales in the fridge, and what Salt Lake's altitude does to all of it.
questions: A recipe says a two inch roast needs about twice as long as a one inch roast. Using how heat diffuses into food, explain why that estimate is wrong, and why a very hot oven makes the overcooked outer band worse.
Why does a wet or crowded surface prevent browning even in a very hot pan, and if searing doesn't seal in juices, what is the actual reason to sear?

Steak and brisket are both beef. In terms of muscle fiber proteins and collagen, why should one be cooked fast and stopped early while the other needs hours, and why is a brisket pulled at a normal 'done' temperature tough?
Why does mayonnaise end up thick and spoonable when it's made of oil and a watery liquid, and why must the first oil go in drop by drop?
Bread goes stale after a day in the fridge but weighs almost the same. What happened inside it, why did the fridge speed that up, and why does warming it in the oven temporarily help?

title: Haber-Bosch: how a catalyst pulls bread out of the air
summary: Why dinitrogen is so inert, the thermodynamics-versus-kinetics trap in ammonia synthesis, what the iron surface and its promoters actually do, the Sabatier principle and volcano plots, how Bosch industrialized Haber's lab result, and how nitrogenase does it at room temperature.
questions: A catalyst can't change the equilibrium yield of ammonia. So why does a better catalyst still increase how much ammonia you get from each pass through the reactor?
Why does raising the pressure help the ammonia yield while raising the temperature hurts it, even though both make molecules collide more often?
By the Sabatier principle, why would a metal that binds nitrogen atoms much more strongly than iron be a worse catalyst, even though it splits nitrogen more easily?
In Bosch's reactor, what did hot hydrogen do to ordinary steel, and why did a low-carbon inner liner with a vented outer shell solve it?
Nitrogenase works at room temperature, so why isn't it simply more efficient than the industrial process? What does it spend instead of heat, and where is the waste?

title: Robert Moses: how one unelected man ran a city for forty years
summary: How Robert Moses built durable power without votes: bill drafting, public authorities that compounded toll revenue into new bonds, covenants shielded by the contract clause, and the threat to resign. Then the costs, the tangled low-bridge story, his fall through Rockefeller and Chase Manhattan, and the three faces of power.
questions: The original idea of a public authority was that it would pay off its bonds and wind down. Explain how Moses turned Triborough into something that grew instead, and why that growth made him harder to remove.
Why could a bond covenant protect a public official from an elected legislature? What role does the contract clause play, and why did it matter that new bonds kept being issued?
Why was the identity of the bondholders' trustee so important to Rockefeller's ability to merge Triborough into the MTA?
Robert Dahl studied the decisions that got fought over and concluded power was spread out. Using the second face of power, explain what a study like that would have missed about Moses.
The low-bridge story is often told as simple deliberate exclusion. What does the careful version say is well established, what remains uncertain, and why?

title: Weather forecasting: Richardson's failure, Lorenz's wall, and the machines
summary: Numerical weather prediction as an initial value problem: why Richardson's hand forecast blew up, the Courant Friedrichs Lewy cost of resolution, Lorenz chaos and the two-week limit, data assimilation as GPS-style least squares, ensembles, and what machine learning models did and did not change.
questions: Richardson's method was essentially correct, yet his six-hour forecast predicted a wildly unrealistic pressure change. What went wrong with his initial state, and why did a small error in the observed winds produce such a large error in the pressure tendency?
Why does halving the grid spacing of a weather model cost far more than twice the computing power? What role does the Courant Friedrichs Lewy condition play?

Why is the forecast-length gain from better initial measurements logarithmic rather than proportional, and why does Lorenz's multi-scale argument say even perfect measurement would not push the horizon out indefinitely?

In data assimilation, how can a single wind observation over the ocean improve the estimate of the pressure field there, which was never measured? Connect it to how a GPS receiver handles its clock error.
Why does a deterministic neural forecast trained on average squared error get blurrier at long lead times even while its scores stay good, and how do ensemble or probabilistic approaches address it?

title: Why the Roman Republic fell: a constitution that ran on restraint
summary: The fall of the Roman Republic as institutional failure: a high-veto system held together by unwritten norms, the Gracchi and the first political killings, the emergency decree, why the 'Marian reforms' are mostly a modern myth, Sulla's march and failed fix, and the road to the Rubicon, including the debate over Caesar's motives and whether the collapse was structural or contingent.
questions: The Republic gave enormous blocking power to individual officials, especially the tribunes. Why did a system with that many veto points work for centuries, and what is the mechanism by which heavy use of vetoes leads not to permanent gridlock, but to the rules being bypassed?

The senatus consultum ultimum was legally only advice. Why was it nonetheless so powerful, and why did it end up making the situation worse rather than better? Use Cicero's execution of the Catilinarian conspirators and his later exile in your answer.

The popular account says Marius created armies loyal to their generals by recruiting the poor. What is wrong with that story, and what is the more accurate mechanism that tied soldiers' loyalty to individual commanders?

Sulla tried to restore senatorial control and then voluntarily gave up power. Why did his reforms fail to last, while his march on Rome had lasting effects? What does that say about the relationship between written rules and precedent?

Compare two views of the fall: a long structural decline beginning in 133, versus Gruen's argument that the institutions still functioned in the 50s and the collapse came from one specific crisis. What evidence from this lecture supports each side?

title: The jet engine: why it slowly turned back into a propeller
summary: How a modern turbofan works, built from two competing efficiencies: thrust as momentum and where the force really acts, the Brayton cycle and pressure ratio, why compressors need many stages (adverse pressure gradients and stall), running turbine blades above their melting point, propulsive efficiency and bypass ratio, and the limits of the fan, from geared turbofans to open rotors.
questions: A jet engine is tested in a vacuum chamber with nothing behind it. Does it produce more, less, or the same thrust as the same exhaust in air, and where on the engine does the forward force actually act?

Raising the compressor pressure ratio raises the ideal cycle efficiency. Why, at a fixed maximum turbine temperature, does pushing the pressure ratio ever higher eventually stop paying off, and what happens to the power per kilogram of air?
Why does a high pressure compressor need roughly ten stages while the turbine driving it needs only one or two? Answer in terms of the boundary layer and the direction of the pressure gradient.

Using the relationship between thrust and wasted kinetic energy, explain why moving more air more slowly is more efficient. Then explain why that logic does not lead a supersonic fighter to use a high bypass engine.
What problem does the gearbox in a geared turbofan solve? Explain what the fan wants, what the low pressure turbine wants, and why they cannot both have it on a single shaft.

title: How languages are built, and why some are hard for English speakers
summary: Languages as systems of a few design choices: phoneme categories and the perceptual magnet, isolating versus agglutinative versus fusional words, case versus word order and Greenberg's head-direction patterns, what the Foreign Service Institute difficulty ranking really measures, and what research says works for adult learners (input, output, explicit instruction, spaced retrieval).
questions: A Japanese adult has trouble hearing the difference between English r and l. Why is it not just that the sounds are unfamiliar, but that perception is actively pulled toward a single category?
Turkish has many more word endings than Spanish, yet its morphology is in some ways easier to learn. What difference between agglutinative and fusional systems explains that?
English uses fairly rigid word order while Russian and Finnish allow freer order. What is the connection to case marking, and why did losing case endings make fixed order more necessary in English?
Verb-final languages tend to use postpositions and put relative clauses before the noun. What is the processing explanation for why these features travel together?
Why does comprehension fall off sharply at ninety percent word coverage rather than declining gently, and why does Swain's work with immersion students suggest input alone is not enough?

title: Public-key cryptography: from clock arithmetic to RSA and the quantum threat
summary: How strangers share secrets in public: Diffie-Hellman and the discrete logarithm, Euler's theorem and why RSA decryption works, how real RSA breaks (padding oracles, shared primes found by a greatest common divisor), Shor's algorithm as period finding by interference, and the lattice-based replacements already deployed. Opens with a callback on GPS dual-frequency ionosphere correction.
questions: In RSA, why does raising the message to the public exponent and then to the private exponent give the message back? What role does the totient play, and why does knowing the two primes let you compute the private exponent when the public cannot?
Suppose factoring were perfectly hard. Why would textbook RSA, without padding, still be insecure? Give at least one concrete attack, and say what randomized padding fixes.
Two routers generated RSA keys with poor randomness and share one prime factor. How does an attacker recover both private keys without factoring either modulus, and why is that fast?

In Shor's algorithm, why does finding the period of a random number's powers, modulo the modulus, hand you a factor? And why is 'a quantum computer tries every answer at once' the wrong explanation of the speedup?

Why is migrating key exchange to post-quantum cryptography more urgent than migrating signatures, and why do deployments run a classical and a post-quantum key exchange together rather than switching outright?

title: The Cuban Missile Crisis: game theory, groupthink, and the secret deal
summary: The thirteen days as a laboratory for theories of decision-making: chicken and Schelling's threat that leaves something to chance, the Trollope-ploy myth and the secret Jupiter trade, Allison's three models, Janis's groupthink and what the tapes revised, and the near misses (tactical warheads, Black Saturday, submarine B-59) neither leader knew about.
questions: In the game of chicken, why can a player gain by visibly reducing their own options, like throwing away the steering wheel? And what makes such a commitment credible rather than a bluff?
Explain Schelling's idea of the threat that leaves something to chance. Why might a leader deliberately create a risk he cannot fully control, and how does the quarantine fit that description?
What was the Trollope ploy story, and why do historians now call it misleading? How does the secret Jupiter deal change the crisis from a pure game of chicken into a different kind of bargain?
Using Allison's organizational process model, explain why the Soviet missile sites were relatively easy to spot from the air. Why does a rational actor model struggle to explain the same fact?

Janis held up the Missile Crisis as the cure for groupthink. Give one reason from psychology research and one from the historical record why that showcase is weaker than it first appeared. And why is 'it ended peacefully, so the decisions were good' a flawed inference?

title: How a language model is trained: from tokens to gradient descent
summary: The full pipeline behind large language models: byte pair tokenization, next-token prediction as compression, attention and the transformer, backpropagation and Adam across thousands of chips, scaling laws and the Chinchilla correction, and post-training with human feedback and checkable rewards.
questions: Why do language models use subword tokens rather than whole words or single characters? And how does that choice explain why a model can struggle to count the letters in a word?

The training loss is the negative logarithm of the probability assigned to the correct next token. Why does that loss punish a confident wrong answer so much more than a hesitant one? And why can minimizing it force a model to learn structure that nobody explicitly taught it?
Walk through what attention does with queries, keys and values. Why does its cost grow with the square of the context length?

Given a fixed training compute budget, what did the Chinchilla paper conclude about how to split it between model size and training data? And why might a lab deliberately train a smaller model well past that point anyway?
In reinforcement learning from human feedback, why is there a penalty for drifting too far from the original model? What would go wrong without it?

title: How a bill actually becomes law: what the civics version leaves out
summary: Past the cartoon: the funnel of bills, who drafts them and what committees do, the House Rules Committee and the discharge petition's revival, the Senate's unanimous consent, holds and sixty-vote cloture, shell bills and the veto, and where law really gets made: must-pass vehicles, reconciliation and the Byrd rule, and the Congressional Review Act.
questions: In the Senate, why did the move to a two-track system in the early nineteen-seventies make the filibuster more common rather than less, even though it made the Senate more productive in the short run?

The Speaker of the House rarely loses floor votes on major bills. Explain how the Rules Committee and the special rule give the majority leadership that control, and why the vote on the rule matters as much as the vote on the bill.

Why has the discharge petition become a working tool in the current Congress when for most of its history it rarely produced a law? What does that tell you about where the Speaker's power actually comes from?

Budget reconciliation lets a bill pass the Senate with a simple majority. What stops a majority from putting any policy it wants into a reconciliation bill, and how does that constraint end up shaping the design of the laws that pass this way?
Why does the President's veto power do most of its work before a bill ever reaches the President's desk? And why can Congress not override a pocket veto?

title: How MRI works: from a whisper of spinning protons to a picture
summary: Larmor precession and why protons don't just 'flip', resonance in the rotating frame, the two relaxation clocks and Hahn's spin echo, gradients and k-space (why the scanner measures the Fourier transform of you), then parallel imaging, compressed sensing and what functional MRI really sees.
questions: The radio pulse has to be at the Larmor frequency to tip the magnetization. Explain why, using the rotating frame, and say what happens to a pulse that is off-frequency.

A spin echo recovers signal lost to an imperfect magnet but not signal lost to true transverse decay. What is the difference between those two kinds of dephasing that lets the hundred and eighty degree pulse undo one and not the other?
Why does the scanner end up measuring the Fourier transform of the image rather than the image itself? Connect it to what a gradient does to the phase of spins at different positions.
If a patient breathes during a scan, MRI tends to produce ghost copies of the anatomy instead of a simple blur. Why?
In functional MRI, active brain tissue uses more oxygen, yet the signal goes up rather than down. Explain the mechanism, and say what that implies about what functional MRI actually measures.

title: How science actually works: Popper, Kuhn, and one funeral at a time
summary: Hume's problem of induction, Popper's falsification and the real story of the 1919 eclipse, the Duhem-Quine problem through Neptune and Vulcan, Kuhn's paradigms and revolutions, Lakatos's research programmes, and the sociology: Merton's norms, the 'one funeral at a time' study, and the replication crisis as a failure of refutation.
questions: Popper said a single counterexample can refute a universal law, but in practice scientists rarely abandon a theory over one failed prediction. Using the Duhem-Quine problem, explain why the logic doesn't force them to, and why that isn't simply stubbornness.

The Neptune prediction and the Vulcan prediction were the same kind of move. Using Lakatos's framework, explain what distinguishes a progressive adjustment from a degenerating one, and why that distinction is easier to apply in hindsight.

Kuhn argued that the dogmatism of normal science is actually productive. What is the mechanism? Why might a community that refuses to question its foundations be better at discovering that those foundations are wrong?

In the 'one funeral at a time' study, why did the researchers focus on stars who died suddenly rather than all stars who died, and what does the result tell us, and not tell us, about whether the star's ideas were correct?
Explain how flexibility in data analysis connects to Popper's criticism of Adler, and why preregistration addresses the problem at its root rather than just catching bad actors.
